statement: Two students are chosen from a group of six to represent the class. How many different pairs are possible?

choices.misconception: I doubled the group size instead of counting pairs.
I allowed a student to be paired with themselves, adding six impossible pairs.
I counted each pair twice, once in each order, and forgot to halve.
I multiplied 6 by 6, counting every ordered pair including a student with themselves.

hints: Count the ordered choices first: six options for the first student, five for the second. Then ask how many times each unwanted pair got counted, and correct for it.
6 x 5 = 30 ordered choices, but each pair appears twice, so 30 divided by 2 = 15.

solutions.reliable: Choosing in order gives 6 x 5 = 30. But representing the class is not an ordered job - picking Ana then Bo is the same pair as Bo then Ana - so every pair has been counted twice. Halving gives 15. The transferable idea: when order does not matter, count the ordered version and divide by the number of orders.
solutions.elegant: Each of the 6 students pairs with 5 others, giving 30 ends of pairs, and each pair has two ends: 15.

whyOnTest: Selections and arrangements look identical on the page; only the word order tells them apart, and forgetting to halve is the standard slip.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
